# Use MERLIN from another Python project

A project such as PyPNM can depend on MERLIN's native Python package. Installing
the compatible wheel installs the Rust engine and Python extension together;
there is no separate MERLIN desktop application or CLI prerequisite.

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `merlin-ofdm` | Python distribution name used by pip and dependency metadata |
| `merlin` | Module imported by Python code |
| MERLIN Git tag/commit | Source revision from which a wheel is built |
| `merlin*.so` / Windows `.pyd` | Native extension loaded into the Python process |

`pymerlin` is not the package/import name implemented in this checkout. Python
calls the Rust API directly through the extension; it does not launch a binary
or start a sidecar service.

## Quick start: download and install only the Python API

You need **64-bit CPython 3.10** and a wheel for your operating system. The
wheel includes the Rust engine; you do not need the MERLIN desktop application,
CLI, Qt, a Rust compiler or a MERLIN source checkout.

1. Open [MERLIN releases](https://github.com/mgarcia01752/merlin/releases).
2. Open the release you want to use and expand **Assets**. Read its release
   notes for supported platforms and API availability.
3. Download the matching `.whl` file from the table below and that release's
   `SHA256SUMS`. Save them in a `wheels` folder inside your Python project.
   Choose the wheel, not the `.msi`, `.deb`, source ZIP or standalone library.
4. Verify the wheel against its checksum using the
   [release guide](releases.md#download-verify-and-install), then install it
   using the commands below for your operating system.

| Your environment | Wheel filename for the documented version |
| --- | --- |
| Ubuntu 22.04+ x86_64, CPython 3.10 | `merlin_ofdm-0.3.1-cp310-cp310-linux_x86_64.whl` |
| Windows x64, CPython 3.10 | `merlin_ofdm-0.3.1-cp310-cp310-win_amd64.whl` |

These are expected filenames, not a guarantee that a release has published
both assets. If no compatible wheel appears under Assets, use another verified
release or the [source-build instructions](README.md#build-and-install-locally).
Do not rename a wheel to make it match a different Python version or platform.

### Ubuntu: install in your project

Open a terminal in your own project's folder. With CPython 3.10 and its venv
support already installed:

```bash
python3.10 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install --no-index --only-binary=:all: ./wheels/merlin_ofdm-0.3.1-cp310-cp310-linux_x86_64.whl
.venv/bin/python -c "from merlin import Simulation; import merlin; print(merlin.__version__)"
```

### Windows: install in your project

Open **Command Prompt** in your own project's folder. With 64-bit CPython 3.10
and the Python launcher already installed:

```bat
py -3.10 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --no-index --only-binary=:all: .\wheels\merlin_ofdm-0.3.1-cp310-cp310-win_amd64.whl
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -c "from merlin import Simulation; import merlin; print(merlin.__version__)"
```

If your project already has a compatible environment, skip creating `.venv` and
use that environment's Python executable for the install and import check.
When choosing another release, replace the wheel filename with the exact file
you downloaded. Installing this local wheel does not fetch MERLIN from PyPI.

### Copy and paste: install by release tag

Run one block below from your own project's folder. Change only `MERLIN_TAG`
to the published release you want; the version and wheel URL are derived from
it. These commands download the wheel directly into pip and install it in
`.venv`. They do not require a MERLIN checkout or a desktop installer.

Use a release whose Assets contain the matching CPython 3.10 wheel. The default
below follows this document's version; it does not establish asset availability.
A missing asset causes installation to fail. For explicit SHA-256 verification
before installation, use the download-and-verify steps above instead.

**Ubuntu — Bash**, with CPython 3.10 and venv support installed:

```bash
(
    set -e
    MERLIN_TAG="v0.3.1"
    MERLIN_VERSION="${MERLIN_TAG#v}"
    MERLIN_WHEEL="merlin_ofdm-${MERLIN_VERSION}-cp310-cp310-linux_x86_64.whl"
    MERLIN_URL="https://github.com/mgarcia01752/merlin/releases/download/${MERLIN_TAG}/${MERLIN_WHEEL}"

    # Create the project environment, then download and install this release.
    python3.10 -m venv .venv
    .venv/bin/python -m pip install --no-index --only-binary=:all: "$MERLIN_URL"

    # Confirm that the installed package exposes the simulation API.
    .venv/bin/python -c "from merlin import Simulation; import merlin; print(merlin.__version__)"
)
```

**Windows — PowerShell**, with 64-bit CPython 3.10 and the Python launcher
installed (this block is for PowerShell, not Command Prompt):

```powershell
& {
    $MERLIN_TAG = "v0.3.1"
    $MERLIN_VERSION = $MERLIN_TAG -replace '^v', ''
    $MERLIN_WHEEL = "merlin_ofdm-$MERLIN_VERSION-cp310-cp310-win_amd64.whl"
    $MERLIN_URL = "https://github.com/mgarcia01752/merlin/releases/download/$MERLIN_TAG/$MERLIN_WHEEL"

    # Create the project environment, then download and install this release.
    py -3.10 -m venv .venv
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Could not create the Python environment." }
    .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --no-index --only-binary=:all: $MERLIN_URL
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "MERLIN wheel installation failed." }

    # Confirm that the installed package exposes the simulation API.
    .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -c "from merlin import Simulation; import merlin; print(merlin.__version__)"
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "MERLIN API import failed." }
}
```

Tags in these examples use `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, such as `v0.3.1`.
For an existing compatible environment, omit its creation command and replace
`.venv` with that environment's path. Pin the same version in your project as
explained under [Declare a dependency](#declare-a-dependency-in-the-consuming-project).

### Use it in your code

```python
from merlin import Simulation

# Create an idle session; no simulation runs yet.
sim = Simulation()
```

Continue with the [simple Python workflow](README.md#simple-workflow) to load
your modulation profile and RxMER inputs and run the simulation. Example capture
files are separate from the wheel. To make MERLIN part of your project's
installation, follow [Declare a dependency](#declare-a-dependency-in-the-consuming-project).

## Version and availability

The documented package version is **0.3.1** and the corresponding source
release reference is **v0.3.1**. A reference is an expected source pin,
not a claim that the tag already exists or that a wheel has been published.
Verify that the chosen source contains the API and that approved wheel assets
exist before configuring a downstream public dependency.

The Ubuntu target is 22.04+ x86_64 / CPython 3.10. Release CI builds on 22.04
and tests that same wheel on 24.04 and 26.04; new checks remain pending hosted
validation. Its
wheel filename is `merlin_ofdm-0.3.1-cp310-cp310-linux_x86_64.whl`. Each
release needs its own validated artifact. Other platforms and Python ABIs
remain unverified unless that release supplies supporting evidence. A native
`linux_x86_64` wheel does not promise manylinux compatibility.

This document is generated from a tracked template by
`tools/python/update_integration_doc.py`. Every guarded push refreshes or checks
it; release bumps include it in the release commit. Generation does not build
wheels, publish assets, query registries or establish release availability.

The separate [Python wheel release guide](releases.md) describes the configured
Ubuntu/Windows CPython 3.10 asset names and installed-example release gates.
Windows wheel execution and published availability still require successful
native release evidence; configuration alone is not verification.

## Install the current local build

The [build guide](README.md#build-and-install-locally) produces a wheel under
`local/python-wheels/`. Install it into the Python environment used by the
consuming application. This concrete development example uses a fresh local
environment in the MERLIN checkout:

```bash
python3 -m venv local/api-consumer
local/api-consumer/bin/python -m pip install --no-index --only-binary=:all: \
  --find-links local/python-wheels 'merlin-ofdm==0.3.1'
local/api-consumer/bin/python -c 'import merlin; from importlib.metadata import version; print(version("merlin-ofdm")); print(merlin.__file__)'
```

This installs only into that environment. For PyPNM, use its environment's
`python -m pip` with an absolute path to the same wheel folder instead. Install
PyPNM normally in that environment and let its integration code `import merlin`.
PyPNM is an example consumer here; this change does not modify it or add an
actual PyPNM integration feature.

The wheel contains the native shared library. A compatible precompiled wheel
requires neither Rust nor Qt on the consuming machine. Source builds require
Rust and the Python development/build prerequisites.

## Declare a dependency in the consuming project

If simulation is optional, a consumer can declare an extra in its own
`pyproject.toml`. This is an illustrative downstream change, not existing PyPNM
metadata:

```toml
[project.optional-dependencies]
merlin = ["merlin-ofdm==0.3.1"]
```

Merge that declaration into the existing project metadata. If MERLIN is required
for all users, add the exact requirement to the project's existing
`[project].dependencies` instead. Install from a wheelhouse/private package
index containing the approved artifact. Pip then resolves the dependency as part
of installing the consumer; a separate manual first-install step is unnecessary.
See the official [Python dependency/extra guide](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/writing-pyproject-toml/)
and [pip installation reference](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/cli/pip_install/).

For local consumer development, after adding that illustrative extra:

```bash
# Run in the consuming project's checkout, using its own environment.
python -m pip install --find-links /absolute/path/to/merlin/local/python-wheels '.[merlin]'
```

That command may fetch the consumer's other dependencies from its configured
index. A fully offline installation needs a wheelhouse for every dependency.
Keep the MERLIN feature's import inside its integration module so users who
omit an optional extra can still use the rest of the application.

## Pin a release version or tag

The normal delivery sequence is:

1. MERLIN commits and tags a version containing the API.
2. A maintainer builds and tests compatible wheels from that exact source
   revision, including licenses/notices and SHA-256 checksums.
3. The approved artifacts become available through a package index, release
   assets or a supplied wheelhouse.
4. The consumer pins the matching package version or exact wheel URL/hash.

Check the chosen release to establish whether those steps have completed.
A Git tag identifies source; installing a wheel selects the version, platform
and Python ABI together. The wheel version must match the intended source tag.
For long-term provenance, record both the immutable source commit and artifact
SHA-256 alongside the consumer's dependency lock.

For future GitHub-release delivery, a pip requirement can use an exact published
wheel URL with its SHA-256 fragment. Use the actual tested asset URL and digest;
do not derive an asset URL merely from a version number. A single wheel URL
is platform-specific, so do not treat one Linux wheel as a universal dependency.
Package-index delivery lets pip choose the compatible wheel for a version.

For reproducible deployment from a wheelhouse, use a locked requirement such as:

```text
merlin-ofdm==0.3.1 --hash=sha256:<VERIFIED_WHEEL_SHA256>
```

Replace `<VERIFIED_WHEEL_SHA256>` with the verified digest for the exact wheel
you distribute; this is a template, not an installable lock line.
[Validation](../../development/features/high-level-api/validation.md) records
previous local artifacts, not checksums for every future release. Rebuilding
may change an artifact's hash. Update deployment locks only after verification.
Pip's [repeatable installation](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/topics/repeatable-installs/)
guide explains version and artifact locking; hashes must cover all dependencies
when using hash-checking mode for a full environment.

## Build from a pinned source revision

When an API-bearing tag/commit is available, obtain that full MERLIN source
revision, install the pinned build prerequisites, and run the repository's
`tools/python/build_wheel.py` helper as described in the [build guide](README.md).
Keep the complete checkout: the adapter has relative dependencies on Rust crates
outside `bindings/python`. The helper also generates complete dependency notices.
Then install the resulting wheel into the consumer's environment.

Do not use a moving branch as a deployment pin. Direct `pip install git+...` from
the adapter subdirectory is not the validated distribution route and bypasses
the helper's notice-generation step. The consumer does not need a source
checkout or Rust compiler when installing the approved prebuilt wheel.

After installation, run the [Python API example](../../../examples/api/python/run_single_capture.py)
and the consuming application's own integration tests. Installing a dependency
alone does not implement PyPNM's application-level use of MERLIN.

Return to the [Python guide](README.md) or [documentation index](../../README.md).
